\section{Introduction}

SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.

We provide this analysis.
The gradient of BCE with respect to neuron $j$'s score is $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$, a function of $j$ alone, independent of every other neuron.
Under KL divergence, the gradient for neuron $j$ in layer $\ell$ factors as:
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}}{\partial s_j^{(\ell)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}}{\partial \mathbf{z}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}}{\partial \tilde{m}_j^{(\ell)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \tilde{m}_j^{(\ell)}}{\partial s_j^{(\ell)}},
\end{equation*}
where the Jacobian $\partial \mathbf{z} / \partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}$ propagates through all downstream layers, coupling each neuron's gradient to every other neuron's mask state.
This structural difference predicts that KL should outperform BCE specifically under global allocation, and the prediction is confirmed empirically: BCE achieves higher oracle F1 (0.613 vs.\ 0.540) yet produces 137\% worse perplexity, because per-neuron magnitude accuracy is a misaligned proxy for output-distribution preservation.

To test whether end-to-end distillation can overcome this mismatch, we instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
With uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.96 at 50\% sparsity; under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\% over TEAL) but late-layer starvation amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\times$), motivating uniform allocation for deployment.
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} confirms consistent improvements at the 7--8B scale (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy} situates prior work along correction granularity and training signal coupling).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item Quantitative characterization of the structural mismatch between per-neuron BCE training and global top-$k$ inference allocation, supported by oracle F1 decomposition and gradient SNR measurements (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
\item Empirical validation that KL distillation overcomes this mismatch for activation sparsity, revealing that oracle F1 and perplexity are inversely decoupled: BCE achieves +7pp F1 yet 137\% worse PPL (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\item Analysis of how allocation strategy governs the prediction-to-downstream gap, identifying a late-layer starvation mechanism and characterizing qualitative shifts across sparsity levels at the 7--8B scale (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
\end{itemize}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	
6	\paragraph{Model and Predictor.}
7	We evaluate on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}, which uses SwiGLU FFN blocks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} with $d_{\text{model}}=4096$ and $d_{\text{ff}}=14336$ across 32 layers.
8	The sparsity predictor is a two-layer MLP with 2.37M parameters per layer (75.9M total), implemented as Linear($4096 \to 128$) + GELU + Linear($128 \to 14336$), trained to produce per-neuron importance scores that minimize output-distribution divergence under sparsity.
9	
10	\paragraph{Training.}
11	All predictors are trained for 1000 steps on WikiText-103 with sequence length 2048 and batch size 4, using AdamW~\cite{loshchilov2019adamw} with learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, weight decay $5 \times 10^{-2}$, and cosine decay.
12	The KL predictor uses Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} with temperature $\tau=1.0$ annealed to $0.1$ over training.
13	
14	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
15	We report perplexity on WikiText-2~\cite{merity2017pointer} (seq\_len=2048) and downstream accuracy on ARC-Challenge (25-shot), WinoGrande (5-shot), MMLU (5-shot), and GSM8K (8-shot).
16	
17	\paragraph{Inference Protocol.}
18	At inference, the predictor produces per-neuron scores that are passed to TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal}, which distributes the sparsity budget across layers non-uniformly.
19	We term this \textit{predictor-TEAL}: the predictor replaces TEAL's magnitude-based scoring while retaining its allocation strategy.
20	
21	\paragraph{Baselines.}
22	We compare against: (1) \textbf{Vanilla TEAL}~\cite{liu2025teal}, which uses activation magnitudes directly; (2) \textbf{BCE predictor} (DejaVu-style~\cite{liu2023dejavu}), trained with per-neuron binary cross-entropy on magnitude-based oracle masks for 1000 and 2700 steps; (3) \textbf{Uniform allocation}, which distributes the sparsity budget equally across layers; and (4) \textbf{WINA}~\cite{liu2025teal}, an importance-weighted variant.
23	
24	
25	\subsection{Main Results}
26	
27	Table~\ref{tab:main} presents the primary comparison. We recommend uniform allocation for deployment (best downstream preservation); global allocation is analyzed to understand allocation-quality tradeoffs (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
28	At 30\% sparsity, KL distillation with global TEAL allocation achieves PPL 8.98, reducing TEAL's degradation from dense (10.97 $\to$ 8.98, an 18\% improvement). % exp_id: kl_30_global_teal
29	The advantage holds across additional downstream benchmarks (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
30	Uniform allocation at 30\% provides stable downstream performance (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed) while global top-$k$ exhibits high seed variance (35.7$\pm$9.5\%), with late-layer starvation (L31 retention 28.4\%) interacting with predictor initialization (\S\ref{sec:scaling}). % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, kl30_3seed
31	
32	At 50\% sparsity, KL distillation over vanilla TEAL widens the PPL advantage: 11.79 vs.\ 23.31, a 49\% reduction. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, bench_teal50
33	The predictor also generalizes to held-out data (C4 validation: 52.5\% advantage over TEAL; see Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
34	However, all methods exhibit downstream collapse on MMLU (28.1$\pm$0.2\% vs.\ 28.0$\pm$0.6\%, both $\approx$ random, 3-seed) and GSM8K ($<$2.2\%), indicating a capacity-limited regime where no allocation strategy can recover. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, d030_kl50_uniform, multi_seed_kl50_global
35

TEAL~\cite{liu2025teal} applies global top-$k$ selection by activation magnitude, achieving 40--50\% sparsity with no training cost.

All training-free methods determine masks from fixed statistics or input-independent criteria, while our predictor generates \emph{input-dependent} masks trained to minimize output-distribution divergence.

\paragraph{Predictor-Based Contextual Sparsity.}
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} introduced learned sparsity predictors trained via BCE to classify each neuron independently.
ShadowLLM~\cite{akhauri2024shadowllm} uses attention-based routing with per-layer MSE supervision, providing intermediate coupling within each layer but no end-to-end gradient signal.
FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} adds a 67.2M-parameter compensation network using BCE for mask prediction, adding inference latency.
SVD-CSP~\cite{serbin2026svdcsp} compresses sparsity predictors via SVD decomposition for reduced predictor overhead.
PowerInfer~\cite{song2024powerinfer} exploits power-law activation frequencies for GPU--CPU scheduling.
MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} also employs learnable masks with Gumbel relaxation and frozen weights, but targets N:M semi-structured \emph{weight} sparsity (2:4 patterns) via per-group categorical selection (Gumbel-Softmax), producing fixed masks independent of input tokens.
Both share the principle of frozen weights + learnable masks + KL training, but solve distinct optimization problems: MaskLLM finds optimal static N:M patterns within fixed groups, while we predict dynamic per-token masks under a global budget constraint.
The structural mismatch we characterize (per-neuron gradient decomposition vs.\ global top-$k$) does not arise in MaskLLM's per-group categorical setting, where N:M patterns eliminate cross-group budget competition.
All prior predictor-based methods use decomposed (BCE) or intermediate (MSE) objectives where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
Our contribution is primarily empirical: we observe that a coupled KL objective propagates gradients through all downstream layers and quantify when this matters for global allocation quality.

\paragraph{Static Bias Correction.}
SPON~\cite{xu2026spon} learns input-independent bias vectors via closed-form KL minimization per layer, absorbed into weights at deployment.
Our method is fundamentally different: a per-token contextual predictor trained end-to-end across all layers, producing input-dependent masks.

MiniTron~\cite{muralidharan2024minitron} combines structured pruning with distillation but modifies architecture permanently.
All require retraining or weight modification; our method is a plug-in predictor on \emph{unmodified} SwiGLU models.

\paragraph{Weight Pruning, Distillation, and Routing.}
Wanda~\cite{sun2024wanda} and SparseGPT~\cite{frantar2023sparsegpt} produce static weight masks; Switch Transformers~\cite{fedus2022switch} and Mixture-of-Depths~\cite{raposo2024mod} achieve conditional computation through learned routing.

\section*{Limitations}

Our primary evaluation uses WikiText-2 perplexity, and downstream benchmarks reveal that perplexity is a poor proxy for reasoning ability at moderate sparsity: 40\% sparsity achieves PPL 8.36 but MMLU already degrades, motivating 30\% as the recommended operating point for downstream fidelity.
Training requires 1000 steps on WikiText-103 ($\sim$45 minutes on RTX PRO 6000 for KL, $\sim$17 minutes for BCE), but a separate predictor must be trained for each sparsity target.
All experiments use 7--8B parameter models (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3); scaling behavior to 13B or 70B models remains untested.
Out-of-distribution evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}) covers only 50\% sparsity on C4; extending to 30\% and 70\% is left to future work.
Our attribution of KL's advantage to gradient coupling (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}) is supported by SNR measurements and the BCE isolation ablation, but does not fully disentangle coupling from oracle quality: BCE uses magnitude-based oracles while KL directly optimizes output preservation, and an ablation using KL-derived masks as BCE targets would more precisely isolate the coupling effect.
At 30\% sparsity, global allocation exhibits 9.5pp cross-seed MMLU standard deviation (3-seed), indicating that allocation strategy interacts with predictor initialization in task-specific ways; this variance is MMLU-specific, as ARC, WinoGrande, and GSM8K show stable performance across seeds under both allocation strategies.
While we motivate our work with inference speedup potential, actual wall-clock acceleration depends on sparse kernel implementations (e.g., Triton, cuSPARSE) and hardware-specific memory access patterns; this work focuses on prediction quality rather than systems optimization.
Future directions include N:M structured sparsity for hardware-native acceleration, scaling to 13B+ models, and training a single predictor that serves multiple sparsity targets simultaneously.

\section{Introduction}

SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.

We provide this analysis.
The gradient of BCE with respect to neuron $j$'s score is $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$, a function of $j$ alone, independent of every other neuron.
Under KL divergence, the gradient for neuron $j$ in layer $\ell$ factors as:
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}}{\partial s_j^{(\ell)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}}{\partial \mathbf{z}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}}{\partial \tilde{m}_j^{(\ell)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \tilde{m}_j^{(\ell)}}{\partial s_j^{(\ell)}},
\end{equation*}
where the Jacobian $\partial \mathbf{z} / \partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}$ propagates through all downstream layers, coupling each neuron's gradient to every other neuron's mask state.
This structural difference predicts that KL should outperform BCE specifically under global allocation, and the prediction is confirmed empirically: BCE achieves higher oracle F1 (0.613 vs.\ 0.540) yet produces 137\% worse perplexity, because per-neuron magnitude accuracy is a misaligned proxy for output-distribution preservation.

To test whether end-to-end distillation can overcome this mismatch, we instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
With uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.96 at 50\% sparsity; under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\% over TEAL) but late-layer starvation amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\times$), motivating uniform allocation for deployment.
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} confirms consistent improvements at the 7--8B scale (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy} situates prior work along correction granularity and training signal coupling).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item Quantitative characterization of the structural mismatch between per-neuron BCE training and global top-$k$ inference allocation, supported by oracle F1 decomposition and gradient SNR measurements (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
\item Empirical validation that KL distillation overcomes this mismatch for activation sparsity, revealing that oracle F1 and perplexity are inversely decoupled: BCE achieves +7pp F1 yet 137\% worse PPL (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\item Analysis of how allocation strategy governs the prediction-to-downstream gap, identifying a late-layer starvation mechanism and characterizing qualitative shifts across sparsity levels at the 7--8B scale (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Training-Free Activation Sparsity.}
TEAL~\cite{liu2025teal} applies global top-$k$ selection by activation magnitude, achieving 40--50\% sparsity with no training cost.
CATS~\cite{lee2024cats} adapts per-layer thresholds for SiLU/SwiGLU activations; R-Sparse~\cite{zhang2025rsparse} predicts sparsity from rank-aware SVD projections; DIP~\cite{federici2025dip} combines dynamic input pruning with cache-aware masking; SparseInfer~\cite{shin2025sparseinfer} predicts activation sparsity patterns from attention outputs without additional training.
All training-free methods determine masks from fixed statistics or input-independent criteria, while our predictor generates \emph{input-dependent} masks trained to minimize output-distribution divergence.

\paragraph{Predictor-Based Contextual Sparsity.}
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} introduced learned sparsity predictors trained via BCE to classify each neuron independently.
ShadowLLM~\cite{akhauri2024shadowllm} uses attention-based routing with per-layer MSE supervision, providing intermediate coupling within each layer but no end-to-end gradient signal.
FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} adds a 67.2M-parameter compensation network using BCE for mask prediction, adding inference latency.
SVD-CSP~\cite{serbin2026svdcsp} compresses sparsity predictors via SVD decomposition for reduced predictor overhead.
PowerInfer~\cite{song2024powerinfer} exploits power-law activation frequencies for GPU--CPU scheduling.
MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} also employs learnable masks with Gumbel relaxation and frozen weights, but targets N:M semi-structured \emph{weight} sparsity (2:4 patterns) via per-group categorical selection (Gumbel-Softmax), producing fixed masks independent of input tokens.
Both share the principle of frozen weights + learnable masks + KL training, but solve distinct optimization problems: MaskLLM finds optimal static N:M patterns within fixed groups, while we predict dynamic per-token masks under a global budget constraint.
The structural mismatch we characterize (per-neuron gradient decomposition vs.\ global top-$k$) does not arise in MaskLLM's per-group categorical setting, where N:M patterns eliminate cross-group budget competition.
All prior predictor-based methods use decomposed (BCE) or intermediate (MSE) objectives where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
Our contribution is primarily empirical: we observe that a coupled KL objective propagates gradients through all downstream layers and quantify when this matters for global allocation quality.

\paragraph{Static Bias Correction.}
SPON~\cite{xu2026spon} learns input-independent bias vectors via closed-form KL minimization per layer, absorbed into weights at deployment.
Our method is fundamentally different: a per-token contextual predictor trained end-to-end across all layers, producing input-dependent masks.
SPON solves a static per-layer problem; we solve a global dynamic prediction problem. The two are weakly correlated (cosine similarity 0.196, $R^2$=0.038; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\paragraph{Activation Function Engineering.}
ReLU Strikes Back~\cite{mirzadeh2024relu} replaces SiLU with ReLU for $>$90\% natural sparsity; TurboSparse~\cite{song2024turbosparse} and ProSparse~\cite{song2025prosparse} engineer extreme sparsity through activation modifications; the Sparsing Law~\cite{luo2024sparsinglaw} formalizes how activation density increases with training compute.
MiniTron~\cite{muralidharan2024minitron} combines structured pruning with distillation but modifies architecture permanently.
All require retraining or weight modification; our method is a plug-in predictor on \emph{unmodified} SwiGLU models.

\paragraph{Weight Pruning, Distillation, and Routing.}
Wanda~\cite{sun2024wanda} and SparseGPT~\cite{frantar2023sparsegpt} produce static weight masks; Switch Transformers~\cite{fedus2022switch} and Mixture-of-Depths~\cite{raposo2024mod} achieve conditional computation through learned routing.
KL-based distillation~\cite{kim2016sequencekd,sanh2019distilbert,gu2024minillm,agarwal2024gkd} trains compact students; SparseLoRA~\cite{khaki2025sparselora} exploits contextual sparsity for fine-tuning.
We apply the KL principle to train a sparsity predictor on unmodified dense models, using Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling~\cite{maddison2017concrete,louizos2018l0} for differentiable discrete mask optimization.

\section*{Limitations}

Our primary evaluation uses WikiText-2 perplexity, and downstream benchmarks reveal that perplexity is a poor proxy for reasoning ability at moderate sparsity: 40\% sparsity achieves PPL 8.36 but MMLU already degrades, motivating 30\% as the recommended operating point for downstream fidelity.
Training requires 1000 steps on WikiText-103 ($\sim$45 minutes on RTX PRO 6000 for KL, $\sim$17 minutes for BCE), but a separate predictor must be trained for each sparsity target.
All experiments use 7--8B parameter models (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3); scaling behavior to 13B or 70B models remains untested.
Out-of-distribution evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}) covers only 50\% sparsity on C4; extending to 30\% and 70\% is left to future work.
Our attribution of KL's advantage to gradient coupling (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}) is supported by SNR measurements and the BCE isolation ablation, but does not fully disentangle coupling from oracle quality: BCE uses magnitude-based oracles while KL directly optimizes output preservation, and an ablation using KL-derived masks as BCE targets would more precisely isolate the coupling effect.
At 30\% sparsity, global allocation exhibits 9.5pp cross-seed MMLU standard deviation (3-seed), indicating that allocation strategy interacts with predictor initialization in task-specific ways; this variance is MMLU-specific, as ARC, WinoGrande, and GSM8K show stable performance across seeds under both allocation strategies.
While we motivate our work with inference speedup potential, actual wall-clock acceleration depends on sparse kernel implementations (e.g., Triton, cuSPARSE) and hardware-specific memory access patterns; this work focuses on prediction quality rather than systems optimization.
Future directions include N:M structured sparsity for hardware-native acceleration, scaling to 13B+ models, and training a single predictor that serves multiple sparsity targets simultaneously.

\section*{Limitations}

Our primary evaluation uses WikiText-2 perplexity, and downstream benchmarks reveal that perplexity is a poor proxy for reasoning ability at moderate sparsity: 40\% sparsity achieves PPL 8.36 but MMLU already degrades, motivating 30\% as the recommended operating point for downstream fidelity.
Training requires 1000 steps on WikiText-103 ($\sim$45 minutes on RTX PRO 6000 for KL, $\sim$17 minutes for BCE), but a separate predictor must be trained for each sparsity target.
All experiments use 7--8B parameter models (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3); scaling behavior to 13B or 70B models remains untested.
Out-of-distribution evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}) covers only 50\% sparsity on C4; extending to 30\% and 70\% is left to future work.
Our attribution of KL's advantage to gradient coupling (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}) is supported by SNR measurements and the BCE isolation ablation, but does not fully disentangle coupling from oracle quality: BCE uses magnitude-based oracles while KL directly optimizes output preservation, and an ablation using KL-derived masks as BCE targets would more precisely isolate the coupling effect.
At 30\% sparsity, global allocation exhibits 9.5pp cross-seed MMLU standard deviation (3-seed); allocation strategy interacts with predictor initialization in task-specific ways. this variance is MMLU-specific, as ARC, WinoGrande, and GSM8K show stable performance across seeds under both allocation strategies.
While we motivate our work with inference speedup potential, actual wall-clock acceleration depends on sparse kernel implementations (e.g., Triton, cuSPARSE) and hardware-specific memory access patterns; this work focuses on prediction quality rather than systems optimization.
Future directions include N:M structured sparsity for hardware-native acceleration, scaling to 13B+ models, and training a single predictor that serves multiple sparsity targets simultaneously.
